result: Retroviral lineage tracing in chick embryos specifically labels cardiac neural crest cells and tracks their migration and derivatives. RIA injection at HH9-10 labels premigratory cardiac neural crest cells in the hindbrain, which then migrate through pharyngeal arches and populate cardiovascular structures in a proximal-to-distal progression, with specificity confirmed by HNK-1 co-localization.
evaluation: Claims C25-C33 describe the retroviral labeling methodology and early migration patterns. The approach is well-documented with appropriate temporal controls (C26, C28), anatomical specificity is verified by HNK-1 co-localization (C31-C32), and migration patterns are tracked over time (C29-C30, C33). The figures support the spatial and temporal progression described.

result: Neural crest cells contribute to cardiomyocytes in the ventricular myocardium of chick embryos. RIA-labeled cardiac neural crest cells were observed in known derivatives (pharyngeal arch arteries, aorticopulmonary septum, outflow tract) and, importantly, in the myocardium of ventricles where they express cardiomyocyte markers (Troponin T, Myosin Heavy Chain) without active proliferation or apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C3, C34-C38, C41-C45, C47 collectively demonstrate neural crest contribution to ventricular cardiomyocytes in chick. The retroviral labeling shows YFP+ cells in ventricles expressing cardiomyocyte markers (C42-C43), confirmed by immunostaining (Figure 2C-D). The cells are not proliferating or apoptotic (C44-C45), supporting stable integration. This represents a novel finding (C47) with appropriate controls and marker validation.

result: Neural crest cells contribute to cardiomyocytes in mouse ventricular myocardium. Using Wnt1-Cre lineage tracing (both Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreen and improved Wnt1-Cre2+;R26mTmG lines), neural crest-derived cells were observed in the outflow tract, interventricular septum, and myocardium of both ventricles, representing ~17% of cells in the proximal ventricle, with density decreasing along the proximal-distal axis.
evaluation: Claims C4, C48-C58, C60-C61 demonstrate neural crest contribution to mouse cardiomyocytes using two independent Wnt1-Cre lines (C48-C52), addressing potential ectopic expression concerns (C50-C51). The spatial distribution (C53-C55), temporal stability (C56-C58), and quantification (~17%, C61) are well-documented. The use of the improved Wnt1-Cre2 line strengthens the findings by controlling for known artifacts.

result: Neural crest contribution to ventricular cardiomyocytes is conserved across vertebrates. In chick, mouse, and zebrafish, neural crest cells contribute to trabecular myocardium with similar percentages (~17% in amniotes), decreasing density along the proximal-distal axis, representing a conserved developmental mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C8, C62-C63, C60, C119-C121 synthesize findings across three species. The comparative analysis is supported by consistent quantification (C61, C119-C120), similar spatial patterns (C54, C121), and agreement with prior zebrafish studies (C62, C120). The cross-species validation strengthens the conclusion of evolutionary conservation.

result: sox10 expression is reactivated in zebrafish hearts after injury. Adult zebrafish hearts have few sox10+ cells in the apex under normal conditions, but after ventricular resection, sox10 promoter activity increases by 7 days post-amputation (dpa), with more sox10+ cells present in the regenerating apex by 21 dpa, and these cells contribute to cardiomyocytes.
evaluation: Claims C5, C72-C76, C105 document sox10 reactivation during regeneration using the Tg(-4.9sox10:eGFP) line. The temporal progression is well-documented (C72-C75), with appropriate sham controls (C72), quantification (C76, Supplementary file 1c), and demonstration that sox10+ cells contribute to cardiomyocytes (C105, Figure 4A). The n values are adequate (n=3-6 per condition).

result: Neural crest regulatory genes are upregulated during zebrafish heart regeneration. In situ hybridization shows sox10 and tfap2a transcripts are upregulated after injury and mostly absent in uninjured hearts. sox10 transcripts co-localize with the neural crest lineage marker in Tg(sox10:GAL4-UAS-Cre;ubi-Switch) fish, confirming reactivation in neural crest-derived cells.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C78-C85 demonstrate endogenous upregulation of neural crest genes using in situ hybridization (C78-C81) and lineage tracing (C82-C85). The co-localization experiments (C82-C85) confirm that sox10 reactivation occurs in neural crest-derived lineages. The observation that not all mCherry+ cells are sox10+ at 7 dpa (C85) is appropriately noted and suggests temporal dynamics of gene expression.

result: Transcriptome analysis reveals redeployment of the neural crest gene regulatory network during regeneration. 1093 genes are enriched in sox10+ cells at 21 dpa compared to sox10- cells, including many embryonic neural crest regulatory network genes, cardiomyocyte proliferation genes, and cell cycle genes. The molecular signature of adult sox10+ cells strongly correlates with embryonic neural crest cells.
evaluation: Claims C90-C93, C104 present transcriptome data from FAC-sorted sox10+ vs sox10- cells at 21 dpa. The differential expression analysis identifies 1093 enriched genes (C90, p-adj<0.05), including neural crest regulatory genes (C91, Figure 4D-E), proliferation genes (C92-C93), and shows correlation with embryonic neural crest signature (C104). The experimental design with n=2 biological replicates of 12 pooled ventricles each is reasonable for RNA-seq, though additional replicates would strengthen statistical power.

result: Neural crest-derived cells contribute to zebrafish heart regeneration by redeploying their developmental gene regulatory network. The increased sox10+ cells in regenerating tissue, upregulation of neural crest genes, and expression of proliferation markers suggest that neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes proliferate and contribute to regeneration, though the regenerating population is heterogeneous with both neural crest- and mesoderm-derived cardiomyocytes.
evaluation: Claims C9, C77, C89, C94-C96, C98-C100 propose that neural crest cells contribute to regeneration through gene network redeployment. While the data show sox10 reactivation (C77), gene upregulation (C98), and correlation with developmental programs (C89, C99-C100), several claims are explicitly speculative (C89, C96, C99-C100). The heterogeneity of the regenerating population (C95) and lack of direct lineage tracing during regeneration (only marker reactivation) make it uncertain whether sox10+ cells are proliferating neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes or transdifferentiating cells. Functional experiments (e.g., ablation, proliferation tracking) would be needed to definitively establish causation.

result: The sox10+ cells observed during regeneration are embryonic-derived neural crest progeny that migrate to the injury site. Ablation studies show no post-embryonic neural crest additions to the heart, and the proximal location of sox10-derived cells suggests migration to the wound site after injury.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88, C101-C102 interpret the origin and behavior of sox10+ cells during regeneration. While the ablation data from Abdul-Wajid et al. (C86) supports embryonic origin (C87-C88), the inference about migration (C102) is based on spatial distribution (C101) without direct tracking. The authors appropriately acknowledge alternative possibilities (C103), but definitive evidence for migration vs. local reactivation is lacking. Live imaging or pulse-chase experiments would be needed to confirm migration.

result: The retroviral lineage tracing method overcomes limitations of previous approaches. Quail-chick chimeras may have missed the ventricular contribution due to wound healing delays, difficulty detecting dispersed cells, or altered cell behavior. Previous mouse studies used non-specific markers (P0-cre), while the current study uses the gold-standard Wnt1-Cre marker with improved specificity.
evaluation: Claims C107-C118 provide methodological context and justification. The limitations of quail-chick chimeras (C107-C110) are reasonable explanations for why the contribution was missed, though speculative (C108-C110). The critique of P0-cre specificity (C117) and validation of Wnt1 as the gold standard (C118) are well-supported by citations. The advantages of retroviral labeling (C111-C112) are demonstrated by the results. This contextualizes why the current findings differ from some prior work.

result: Background on cardiac neural crest contributions and methodological limitations. Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to known cardiovascular structures (aorticopulmonary septum, cardiac ganglion, smooth muscle, valves, parasympathetic innervation), and their ablation causes defects resembling human congenital heart defects. Previous lineage tracing methods had inconsistencies due to high background and low resolution, and neural crest contribution to trabecular myocardium was thought to be confined to non-amniotic vertebrates.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C23 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims contextualize the study's motivation and novelty. The known contributions (C1-C2, C17-C20) and ablation phenotypes (C10-C13) are well-documented in the literature. The critique of previous methods (C21-C22) and prior understanding (C23) set up the rationale for the current work.

result: Background on zebrafish heart regeneration and sox10 expression. Adult zebrafish can regenerate hearts after 20% ventricular resection through dedifferentiation and proliferation of pre-existing cardiomyocytes. Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to zebrafish cardiomyocytes during development. The Tg(-4.9sox10:eGFP) line labels neural crest lineages, and sox10 is expressed in migrating cardiac neural crest but downregulated after cells reach the heart.
evaluation: Claims C24, C64-C71 provide established background on zebrafish regeneration and sox10 expression patterns, all supported by appropriate citations. This contextualizes the rationale for examining sox10 reactivation during regeneration and the choice of transgenic line.

result: Neural crest cells contribute to the superior interventricular septum in chick. YFP-labeled cells were observed in this structure, which has been controversial, though ventricular septal defects are common after cardiac neural crest ablation.
evaluation: Claims C38-C40 report a novel observation (C38) in a controversial region (C39). The observation is stated definitively and is consistent with ablation phenotypes (C40). However, the data presentation is limited (mentioned in text but not shown in a dedicated figure panel), and quantification is not provided. While supported, more detailed documentation would strengthen this finding.

result: Comparison with previous zebrafish and mouse studies. Previous zebrafish lineage tracing showed neural crest cells integrate into the primitive heart tube to give rise to cardiomyocytes. The current mouse results are consistent with previous studies using less specific P0-cre lines.
evaluation: Claims C46, C59 contextualize the current findings relative to prior work. The zebrafish comparison (C46) establishes precedent for the chick findings, while the mouse comparison (C59) validates the current results against prior studies despite methodological differences. Both are appropriately cited.

result: Speculations and future directions. Alternative explanations for sox10 reactivation cannot be ruled out. Whether sox10+ cells contribute to other lineages remains unexplored. The findings suggest potential roles in neonatal mouse regeneration and therapeutic approaches for heart repair in mammals, but these require further testing.
evaluation: Claims C103, C106, C122-C124 are explicitly speculative or identify limitations and future directions. These are appropriately qualified by the authors and represent reasonable hypotheses based on the data, but they are not tested in the current study. They serve to contextualize the implications and limitations of the work.
